subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Black Holes: The Basics
description: A short lesson to help you apply Black Holes: The Basics.

hook.text: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing—not even light—can escape.

buildup.text: They form when massive stars collapse at the end of their lives, crushing matter into an impossibly tiny point.

discovery.text: John Michell first imagined 'dark stars' in 1783. Einstein's equations later proved they must exist.

twist.text: Despite their name, black holes aren't holes or empty. They contain enormous mass in an incredibly small volume.

climax.text: In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope captured the first image of a black hole—a glowing ring around darkness.

punchline.text: Not a hole. Not empty. A gravity trap that eats light.

quiz.question: Why can't light escape a black hole?
options: The gravitational pull is so strong that nothing can reach escape velocity
Black holes absorb all electromagnetic wavelengths like a sponge
Light is converted into matter inside the black hole

details.summary: Black holes are regions where gravity is so extreme that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the event horizon. Formed from collapsed massive stars or growing over cosmic time, they range from a few solar masses to billions, shaping galaxies and bending spacetime itself.
details.whyItMatters: Black holes are nature's most extreme objects. They test the limits of physics, anchor entire galaxies, and revealed phenomena like gravitational waves — transforming our understanding of spacetime.
takeaways: Nothing escapes a black hole once past the event horizon
They form from collapsed massive stars or grow over eons
Black holes range from stellar mass to supermassive

faq.question: Can a black hole swallow the entire universe?
faq.answer: No. Black holes don't roam around consuming everything. Their gravitational pull follows the same inverse-square law as any mass. From a safe distance, orbiting a black hole is no different from orbiting a star of equal mass. They only capture matter that ventures too close.

faq.question: What would happen if you fell into a black hole?
faq.answer: For a stellar-mass black hole, tidal forces would stretch you into a thin strand (spaghettification) before you reached the horizon. For a supermassive black hole, you could cross the horizon without noticing — but could never return.
